body: The sun comes in through the Commons’ east windows for the first time since Monday and lands on every wet thing at once: the puddles on the patio, the chrome of the bike rack, the eucalyptus by the dish return, still dripping, each drop lit like a dropped coin on its way down. Half the tables have migrated outside in their coats. A boy in the omelet line is wearing sunglasses indoors, and nobody has the heart.

Jack got here at twenty past and held the table in the sun with the Carhartt and two forks laid crosswise, a Youngstown claim, and by now the claim has filled. Kevin has the clipboard, a blue ballpoint and a quiz face. Margot has a drop slip in front of her and a cup of hot water she hasn’t dressed with anything. And Theo is up before ten on a Friday, which hasn’t happened since the first week of September: Sigma Rho hasn’t let him sleep since Monday, and a gold pin the size of a thumbnail sits on the lapel of the blazer, and Hollis is retired and home in his teacup, and without an egg to be careful of, Theo has become insufferable in a new key.

The television over the cereal bar is on CNN with the sound off. The Mall in Washington is a field of knit hats and signs, and the chyron says MARCH FOR LIFE · WASHINGTON and nothing else. Doug Pruitt, passing under it with a tray of tater tots, stops and tilts his entire body toward the screen. “Dude. Is it this big tomorrow?”
Kevin doesn’t look up from the clipboard. “They’re saying thirty-five thousand. Smaller. Colder.”
“Than *that*?” Doug points a tot at the snow on the Mall.
“It’s the Embarcadero, Doug. The wind has a position.”
Doug lowers himself into the chair at the foot of the table with the tots and thinks about it, visibly. “Dude. Are you watching Conan tonight? It’s the last one.”
“I’m bringing popcorn,” Jack says.
“To where?”
“To a household.”
“He is smiling at a tater tot,” says Margot.
“As a brother —” Theo begins, to the butter.
“You’re a brother tomorrow night,” Jack says.
“I am a brother in my heart, Costigan. Tomorrow is paperwork.”
“What are you dropping?” Kevin asks Margot, because the slip is the kind of thing Kevin can’t leave face-up on a table.
“Organizational Behavior.” She signs the line and caps the pen, a vault door closing. “The syllabus said *synergize*. Page one, under learning outcomes.”
“That’s not grounds.”
“It is the only grounds there is, Kevin. The word is a confession. Also, I’m on the van tomorrow.”
The table looks at her. Doug, to whom the van has not been explained, looks at the table.
“It’s a pro-life march,” Kevin says.

“For science. Newman is my beat this semester, and a fifteen-passenger van is the only room in California a person can’t leave.” She drinks her hot water. “I cleared it with Peter. He asked whether I intended to pray. I said I intended to observe, and he said that was a start.”
“Bring a sandwich,” Kevin tells Jack. He taps the clipboard with the ballpoint. “Bring two. Peter’s stops are a matter of conscience.”

The list is a single sheet in Kevin’s blue hand, fourteen names, and near the bottom three or four of them are in pink marker, in a different hand, written over something crossed out. “Some people signed up late,” Kevin says, fast, and turns the sheet face-down against his chest. But Jack has already read it upside down, and BROUSSARD is on it, high up, in blue. He knew it would be. He said yes anyway.

Before the eggs are cold he takes the RAZR out onto the patio, into the sun, and calls Gloria at home. She picks up on the first ring and says she has been up since five, so there is no waking her, whatever he’s done.
“I need Saturday off.”
“Is it the girl?”
“It’s a march.”
“Against what?”
“For.”
There is the sound of a kettle, and of a woman who has put her whole attention on a kettle in order to think. “Boysenberry going?”
“She doesn’t know yet.”

He lets that sit on the line. In the puddle at his boots the sky is intact, with a gull in it. “Rudy’s nephew has been after a Saturday since Thanksgiving,” Gloria says. “He gets this one.” And then, not unkindly, the way she tells a table its pie is gone: “That’s twice, hon.”

When he comes back in, the table has lost a Theo. Theo has taken his coffee to the next table over, “for the light,” where Laney is sitting alone with a tray, upright, lipsticked, the copper hair pinned up. The two of them are angled toward Jack at an exact and unconvincing angle. Jack looks at the sugar dispenser. Laney looks at the sugar dispenser. They have both settled on it.
“The thing people forget, Delaney,” Theo says, at the volume of a back row, “is that half of *communication* is the *ears*.”
“So true, Theodore.” Laney addresses her fruit cup. “You can’t know what someone’s *feeling* unless you *ask*.”
Jack looks up from his eggs, and they freeze: Theo with the cup halfway to his mouth, Laney with a strawberry on a fork, stopped in the air. Then they go on, worse.
“Ask, Theodore.”
“I’m *asking*, Delaney.”
“Then *listen*.”
“I’m *listening*.”
“Act two,” Margot says, without looking up from the drop slip. “They’ve been rehearsing.”

On the back of Jack’s chair, where it has hung since yesterday afternoon, is a pink umbrella with a scalloped edge and a brass handle. He lifts it off and holds it out across the gap between the tables, and Theo gets up and takes it by the middle, as if it were a flag from a coffin, and turns to the girl eighteen inches away.
“Delaney. Costigan returns the umbrella.”
Laney’s eyes stay on her tray. “Tell Costigan thank you.”
“She says thank you,” Theo says.
“I’m four feet away, Theo.”
Neither of them dignifies it. Laney stands, tray in both hands, chin level, and comes past Jack’s table on the way to the dish return, and says one word at the temperature of the milk. “Costigan.”
She sets a granola bar down on his tray without a sound, carefully, as one sets something down near a man who might slam it, and says, “For the van,” and keeps her eyes on the dish return.

Kevin has turned the clipboard over again. Jack looks at the bar, and at the back of the copper head, and at the bar. In September Laney would have dumped the fruit cup in his lap and called it an accident; in December she wouldn’t say his name in a room. Since the basement she says it constantly, his last name and nothing after it, and then she leaves him a granola bar. He can’t make the two halves into one girl. He has stopped trying to guess which half is the act.

Theo comes back to Jack’s table alone and sits, as though none of it had occurred, and lifts his coffee to the light. “Listening, Costigan,” he says, as if the thought had just arrived. “It’s half of it.”

response: “Everything is about the birthday,” Theo says. “The sheet cake has a subcommittee.” He reaches across and takes the second half of Jack’s toast, as tribute.
“I’m not on the subcommittee,” Kevin says.
“Nobody said you were, Tran. It hasn’t been formed. You are, however, under consideration.”

“We’re being *supportive*,” Theo says. “Of each other. In public. It’s very modern.” He stirs a coffee that has never needed stirring, and Margot’s pen stays capped. Then, short, all the lacquer gone off it: “Eat your eggs, Costigan.”

Jack eats. Theo finishes, and the bit gets longer and worse: the ears, the heart, a thought he attributes to Truffaut that Truffaut did not have, a second movement on the subject of eye contact. It goes on until Kevin says, “He’s eating, Theo,” and Theo sits back, wounded, and steals a tot from Doug’s tray.

body: The alarm Jack set for 4:30 has been dead for eight minutes, and the room is still black, the window a slightly less black square in it. He is sitting on the edge of the bed in the Mooney hoodie, lacing his boots by feel, after three hours and ten minutes of something that was not quite sleep.

Across the room, a shape sits up against the dark: the wine-colored robe, the knees together, the hands on them. On the nightstand the teacup has caught the hall light under the door, with the retired egg in it. Theo has not been woken. Theo, by the posture, has been waiting.

“Item,” Theo says. “Sandwich at hour four, not hour two. Item. The cooler is not furniture. Item. Whatever Peter tells you about the route, he is wrong by eleven minutes, and he will tell you with love. Item.” A pause, and the pitch goes out of his voice, and what is left is short. “Take the window, Costigan. The aisle is for people who want to leave.”
Jack, one boot on: “What?”
Theo doesn’t say it again. He sits in the dark with his hands on his knees, having delivered the line, and the line stays delivered.
Then, too gently for Theo, to the dark: “A man who’s hurt should sit where the light is.” Jack doesn’t answer it. He ties the second boot.

He gets up and finds the Carhartt on the chair, and the two sandwiches in the Ziploc that he built at one in the morning on the desk with a plastic knife, and goes for the door. Behind him a pen cap clicks, a pad tears, a robe moves. Theo is there before the door is open, a feat before noon in the five months Jack has known him, and holds it for him with one hand and claps him on the back with the other, once, flat.
“Godspeed, Father Jack.”
On the stairs, between three and two, he shrugs the jacket straight on his shoulders and something crackles at his back. He reaches around and comes away with a square of yellow paper.

s13v.slug: SATURDAY · 3:10–11:50 PM · US-101 SOUTH — THE BACK BENCH
body: The van comes up out of the garage on Washington Street at ten past three with the signs stacked flat in the back like a deck of very large cards, and the low sun slides down the cross streets at it, and Peter takes the ramp with both hands and a rosary swinging from the mirror.

Lena is on the front bench beside him. She and Kenzie traded places in the garage, and nobody remarked on it; Kenzie, who rode up shotgun with an atlas she didn’t need, was out of the front seat before the sentence was over. She is now in row three at Jack’s shoulder, shining, with the road atlas in her lap and her BlackBerry in her fist.
“Okay, I’m not going to be weird,” she says. “Is she nice? Like nice nice, or TV nice?”
“She ranked four brothers by height out loud.”
“That’s *TV* nice,” Kenzie breathes, in awe.
“Kenzie. She didn’t want anything posted.”

The shine goes off her all at once. She is twenty, and a cantor, and her face was built to be read from the back of a church. “Oh,” she says. “Oh, no. I thought — she stood in front of Clare. I just wanted people to know she was *good*.”
“She is.” It is true, and it is the problem, and he can’t think how to say both halves to a girl holding a BlackBerry like a hymnal. “Leave it up. It’s done.”
Kenzie nods several times. “Can I still ask you something and you won’t get mad?”
“No.”
From the back bench, a hand goes up, white, with a thermos in it. “Costigan,” says Margot. “The back bench has a window and no follow-up questions.”
He is over the cooler and into the last row before Kenzie has finished saying, “Wait, I have *so* many,” and the van slides onto the freeway and sets itself south.

South of the city, with the planes coming in low over the freeway toward the airport, he takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt, and the little screen says 3:30. He shuts it and puts it back. It stays there.
Margot sits beside him with the notebook shut on her knee and the pen capped. She has said nothing for twenty minutes. When she speaks, she keeps her eyes on the Peninsula.
“You said ‘any of this.’ I wrote down ‘this.’”

He looks at the notebook, and then at the side of her face. She doesn’t say anything else, and from Margot that is a mercy. After a while he takes the Ziploc out of the Carhartt and holds it open between them, and Margot inspects the pair and takes the one on the left.
“Peanut butter,” she says. “No jelly.”
“The Commons was out.”
“Then it’s honest.” She eats it in four bites, looking out at the long gray shopping centers, and what she says when it’s gone is, “Acceptable.”
Past Gilroy the garlic comes in through the vents, and Joey identifies it, loudly, by name.
“They make garlic ice cream,” Tyler says, with a missionary’s awe.
“That isn’t a sin,” says Bridget. “It’s a crime.”

By Salinas the light is gone, the lettuce fields are black on both sides, and the windows have turned to mirrors. In the second-to-last row Kevin has been working up to it since the garage; he swivels all the way around in his seat.
“Okay. Before the brothers.” He actually stops. “You didn’t have to ride with us. I know the other car was right there.”
“I said I would.”

“I know you did. I’m saying I know.” It lasts exactly as long as he can stand it. “So, the brothers.” He has the clipboard against his chest, a shield. “Javi, the oldest, asked my intentions. In front of the *Ferry Building*. I said ‘Honorable, sir,’ and he said ‘I’m twenty-seven, don’t call me sir,’ and Luis put me in a headlock, which Clare says is how they say they like you, and Nico asked to see my hands —”
“Your hands.”

“They’re all very hands. Tito didn’t say a word and shook mine for what I’d estimate was nine seconds. And your girlfriend asked Javi one question about Montana, and he has never been so happy in his life.” He drops his voice, which does nothing, because Clare is beside him, and Clare is not fooled. “And Javi said I can come to a Niners game. *The* Niners. At the actual stadium, with the family.”
“It’s a very good stadium,” Clare says. “It’s a bad team.” She is nineteen, with a violinist’s calluses on her left hand, and she hasn’t said much since the man with the megaphone.
Jack leans across the aisle. “Kev. Is a march a date?”
Kevin’s ears go red in the dome light. He doesn’t say anything fast. “It was,” he says.
Clare says nothing. She turns her face to the window, where there is nothing now but the lit inside of the van and a valley behind it, and keeps it there.

Peter stops at the King City Burger King at ten past seven, because the route says so and because Joey has begun to chant. The Burger King is lit like an operating room. The teenager at the register says, “Welcome to Burger King,” to fourteen people who have been looking at one another since five in the morning.

In the lot, under the sign, Jack takes the RAZR out of the Carhartt for the first time since the freeway, and it takes a minute to remember where it is, and then it delivers everything at once. Four texts from Gina, stamped with the hours they were sent, three hours back.

body: Kenzie’s picture has got to Glenwood Avenue. He can see where it landed: the Dell on the kitchen table, and his mother standing over it with her arms folded instead of sitting down, because sitting would mean she was staying. *That’s something.* It is not the sentence he was braced for. And Nonna has done the arithmetic on a stranger’s feet. He laughs, once, a short startled sound in a Burger King parking lot, the first since the curb, and a man in a pickup looks over.

Inside, Becca turns around in the line with her scarf wound twice. Peter’s route gives King City thirty minutes and the word DINNER in bold. “I’m not going to ask,” she tells Jack. “I’m going to tell you I’ve been praying since San Francisco, and I’m not going to say who for. It’s a lot of people for one van. I’ve been doing it in shifts.”

Joey, at the end of the line, has his phone held out at arm’s length like a lantern. The Cavs have been on a scoring site since the lot, and Jack grew up in the half of Ohio that hates Cleveland and makes an exception for one man from Akron.
“GIBSON!” Joey says. The whole restaurant looks up from its fries. “GIBSON! A HUNDRED TO NINETY-NINE! HE HIT THE THREE!”
“Congratulations?” says the teenager at the register.

Jack finds he is on his feet in the middle of a Burger King with his hand in Joey Abruzzo’s, pumping it, and Tyler has started on a chant that has no words, and at the booth by the window Peter has the laminated route out between the trays. Lena is across from him with her finger on a line of it. She looks up, with everyone, at the noise. She looks down.
Peter counts heads in the lot, twice, and gets fourteen, the right number, and they go back out into the dark with the radio low, a ranchera from a station in Salinas that nobody asks him to change.
Somewhere ahead of them on the same road the Saab is going south with its top up and one person in it.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. At the Walk, Clare’s brothers said he can come to a Niners game. I asked him if a march is a date. He said it was. I rode home with him.

choices.text: *Help Kevin hold the signs on the turns.*
response: The stack slides on every curve of the Cuesta Grade. The two of them hold it with their knees, and Kevin explains the physics of it, badly and happily, with the gloves he brought for everybody on his hands at last.
He shuts his eyes against the window. He doesn’t sleep. Somewhere around Santa Maria Margot puts her scarf over his knees and says nothing about it.
He answers the second one, in the dome light of the van, with the signal fading in and out between the ranchos.

body: At five past eight, when Jack woke, Theo’s bed was made. Hospital corners, the blanket squared, the pillow set on it like a hat. When Jack came in from the lot at ten to one, it had been a heap. Whatever hour Theo got in from Sigma Rho’s final rites, and whatever hour he left again, Jack slept through both.

The door bangs open at 10:35 on Theo in running shorts and a sweatshirt gone dark at the neck, his sneakers wet and gray with sand to the ankle, his hair standing up in salt. Jack is at the mirror on the inside of the closet door, fighting a tie.
“I run now,” Theo says.
“Four miles?”
“Four miles. In shoes. I’m evolving.” He drops a bath towel over his head, and speaks from under it. “Do not ask me about last night.”
“How were the rites?”
“There was a goat. I’ve said too much.”

The shower runs. It runs a long time, longer than a goat requires. When Theo comes out he is a brother in the full sense, in a clean shirt and the blazer, with a black-and-gold scarf wound three times at the throat, and he stops in front of the mirror and tugs Jack’s tie into true without comment.
“Doors at noon for the Jets,” he says. “Sully’s. I am going to be correct to Broussard for seven hours.”
“What does that involve?”
“I nod. I say ‘Broussard.’ I use the correct number of degrees.” He sniffs. “Laney says nine is perfect. I am told I am a natural at nine.”
He takes his keys off the desk, and goes to the door, and stops there with his hand on it. When he speaks again there is nothing in it but the question.
“You coming?”
“No.”

Theo looks at him past the end of the bit. Then he nods, the correct number of degrees, and the scarf goes off down the hall. By noon there will be a coat on his chair at the long table under the bell. Jack finishes the knot. It comes out crooked, and he leaves it.
